name: Prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica)
short: Case reports, record review: seeded fruit caused rectal blockage, once with perforation; low blood sugar in a man on diabetes drugs eating crude cactus pads. Trials: gastric intolerance, loose stools.
text: Case reports and a hospital case series describe seed bezoars (hardened masses of seeds) in the rectum after eating prickly pear fruit: an older patient presented with rectal perforation and needed surgery with a colostomy; a 76-year-old woman who ate almost 40 fruits developed faecal impaction; and in a 10-year review of adults hospitalised with faecal impaction at one hospital in Israel, prickly pear seeds made up the bezoar in 12 of the 30 people with seed bezoars, all of whom needed disimpaction under general anaesthesia. These reports concern eating the whole fruit with its seeds, not extracts. A case report describes a man with type 2 diabetes taking metformin and glipizide who had 4 low blood sugar episodes (49 to 68 mg/dL) and reported consuming crude prickly pear cactus pads daily for 2 months; the episodes led to glipizide being stopped, and a month later he reported no further low blood sugar (the abstract does not say whether he kept consuming the pads); the authors rated the reaction probable and suggested additive glucose lowering by the three. A 2015 meta-analysis of randomized trials of Opuntia ficus-indica (5 trials included; the abstract does not say which form or preparation of the plant the trials used) reported adverse events of gastric intolerance and flu symptoms, with no numbers and no comparison with controls in the abstract. In a 1-week randomized, double-blind trial in 60 people with irritable bowel syndrome comparing three doses of extracted nopal fibre powder (described as a cactus plant fibre) with placebo, the 30 g a day dose induced more loose stools (p = 0.027; the abstract does not say compared with which group).
